## Introduction

Neural networks represent complex mathematical models through interconnected nodes and layers. Visualizing these structures helps understand model architecture, data flow, and decision patterns. This post demonstrates how to create interactive neural network visualizations in R using packages that work seamlessly with Quarto Live!

Check out: [Quarto Live](https://r-wasm.github.io/quarto-live) for more details. 

## Sample Data

```{webr}
# Load required libraries
library(neuralnet)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Create sample dataset for demonstration
set.seed(123)
sample_data <- data.frame(
  x1 = runif(100, 0, 1),
  x2 = runif(100, 0, 1)
)

# Create target variable with some pattern
sample_data$y <- with(sample_data, 
  ifelse(x1 + x2 + rnorm(100, 0, 0.1) > 1, 1, 0))

# Display first few rows
head(sample_data)
```

## Creating A Basic Neural Network

The `neuralnet` package provides straightforward functions for building and visualizing neural networks. Feel free to experiment with different architectures by modifying the hidden layer configuration!

```{webr}
# Train a simple neural network
# Try changing the hidden parameter: c(3), c(5), c(3,2), etc.
nn_model <- neuralnet(
  y ~ x1 + x2, 
  data = sample_data,
  hidden = c(3), ## Try c(3, 3)! 
  linear.output = FALSE,
  threshold = 0.01
)

# Basic visualization
plot(nn_model)
```

## Interactive Network Architecture

Users can modify the network structure and observe how architecture changes affect the visualization. Different hidden layer configurations create varying levels of complexity.

```{webr}
# Experiment with different architectures
# Architecture 1: Single hidden layer with 5 nodes
nn_simple <- neuralnet(
  y ~ x1 + x2, 
  data = sample_data,
  hidden = 5,
  linear.output = FALSE,
  threshold = 0.01
)

plot(nn_simple, rep = "best")
```

```{webr}
# Architecture 2: Two hidden layers
# Try modifying the values: c(4,2), c(6,3), c(5,3,2)
nn_deep <- neuralnet(
  y ~ x1 + x2, 
  data = sample_data,
  hidden = c(4, 2),
  linear.output = FALSE,
  threshold = 0.01
)

plot(nn_deep, rep = "best")
```

## Advanced Visualization with Custom Styling

Enhanced visualizations provide better insights into network behavior. Custom plotting functions allow for more detailed analysis of weights and connections.

```{webr}
# Function to create enhanced network visualization
create_enhanced_plot <- function(nn_model, title = "Neural Network") {
  # Extract weights and structure information
  weights <- nn_model$weights[[1]]
  
  # Create a more detailed plot
  plot(nn_model, 
       rep = "best",
       col.entry.synapse = "blue",
       col.entry = "black",
       col.hidden = "lightblue",
       col.hidden.synapse = "red",
       col.out = "lightgreen",
       col.out.synapse = "darkgreen",
       fontsize = 12,
       dimension = 6,
       show.weights = TRUE)
  
  title(main = title, cex.main = 1.2)
}

# Apply enhanced visualization
create_enhanced_plot(nn_model, "Enhanced Neural Network Visualization")
```

## Performance Analysis

Understanding how network architecture affects performance helps in model selection. Users can compare different configurations and their accuracy metrics.

```{webr}
# Function to evaluate network performance
evaluate_network <- function(model, test_data) {
  predictions <- predict(model, test_data)
  predicted_classes <- ifelse(predictions > 0.5, 1, 0)
  actual_classes <- test_data$y
  
  accuracy <- mean(predicted_classes == actual_classes)
  
  return(list(
    accuracy = accuracy,
    predictions = predictions,
    confusion_matrix = table(actual_classes, predicted_classes)
  ))
}

# Create test data
test_data <- data.frame(
  x1 = runif(50, 0, 1),
  x2 = runif(50, 0, 1)
)
test_data$y <- with(test_data, 
  ifelse(x1 + x2 + rnorm(50, 0, 0.1) > 1, 1, 0))

# Evaluate different models
simple_performance <- evaluate_network(nn_simple, test_data)
deep_performance <- evaluate_network(nn_deep, test_data)

# Display results
cat("Simple Network Accuracy:", round(simple_performance$accuracy, 3), "\n")
cat("Deep Network Accuracy:", round(deep_performance$accuracy, 3), "\n")
```

## Interactive Parameter Tuning

Real-time parameter modification demonstrates how different settings affect network behavior. Users can explore various configurations and observe immediate changes.

```{webr}
# Interactive function for building networks with different parameters
build_custom_network <- function(hidden_nodes = 3, threshold = 0.01, stepmax = 1e5) {
  nn <- neuralnet(
    y ~ x1 + x2, 
    data = sample_data,
    hidden = hidden_nodes,
    linear.output = FALSE,
    threshold = threshold,
    stepmax = stepmax
  )
  
  plot(nn, rep = "best")
  
  # Display convergence information
  cat("Convergence achieved:", nn$result.matrix[1,1] < threshold, "\n")
  cat("Steps taken:", nn$result.matrix[3,1], "\n")
  cat("Error:", round(nn$result.matrix[1,1], 6), "\n")
  
  return(nn)
}

# Try different configurations
# Modify these values: hidden_nodes (1-10), threshold (0.1, 0.01, 0.001)
custom_nn <- build_custom_network(hidden_nodes = 4, threshold = 0.01)
```

## Weight Distribution Analysis

Analyzing weight distributions provides insights into network learning patterns. Visualizing weight histograms reveals how the network processes information.

```{webr}
# Function to extract and visualize weights
analyze_weights <- function(nn_model) {
  weights_list <- nn_model$weights[[1]]
  
  # Extract all weights
  all_weights <- unlist(weights_list)
  
  # Create histogram
  hist(all_weights, 
       main = "Distribution of Network Weights",
       xlab = "Weight Values",
       ylab = "Frequency",
       col = "lightblue",
       border = "darkblue",
       breaks = 20)
  
  # Add statistics
  abline(v = mean(all_weights), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  legend("topright", 
         legend = paste("Mean:", round(mean(all_weights), 3)),
         col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  
  # Return summary statistics
  return(summary(all_weights))
}

# Analyze weights from different models
cat("Weight Analysis for Simple Network:\n")
simple_weights_summary <- analyze_weights(nn_simple)
print(simple_weights_summary)
```

## Decision Boundary Visualization

Understanding how neural networks make decisions becomes clearer through boundary visualization. This approach shows how the network separates different classes in the input space.

```{webr}
# Function to create decision boundary plot
plot_decision_boundary <- function(model, data, resolution = 50) {
  # Create grid for decision boundary
  x1_seq <- seq(0, 1, length.out = resolution)
  x2_seq <- seq(0, 1, length.out = resolution)
  grid <- expand.grid(x1 = x1_seq, x2 = x2_seq)
  
  # Predict on grid
  grid_predictions <- predict(model, grid)
  grid$prediction <- as.vector(grid_predictions)
  
  # Create the plot
  ggplot() +
    geom_tile(data = grid, aes(x = x1, y = x2, fill = prediction), alpha = 0.6) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", high = "red", mid = "white", midpoint = 0.5) +
    geom_point(data = data, aes(x = x1, y = x2, color = factor(y)), size = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "blue", "1" = "red")) +
    labs(title = "Neural Network Decision Boundary",
         x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2",
         fill = "Prediction", color = "Actual Class") +
    theme_minimal()
}

# Plot decision boundaries for different models
plot_decision_boundary(nn_simple, sample_data)
```
